fortunes.text: The code you are afraid to touch will soon require modification.
A clear name saves more time than a clever one.
The comment explaining why will outlive the comment explaining what.
Deleting code is a form of design.
The simplest fix is the one you can still explain next month.
Tests describe the behaviour you are willing to defend.
A small function with one job is a kindness to the next reader.
The bug you cannot reproduce is still a bug.
Shipping is a decision, not a mood.
Write down the interface you wish you had before the next change.
Good logging is a letter to your future self.
A dependency is a colleague you did not hire.
The review that feels slow is often the one that prevents an outage.
Consistency beats a new pattern invented at midnight.
If two modules must change together, they are already one idea.
The error message is part of the product.
A note that says fix this later, with nobody named, is only a wish.
Measure the slow part before you rewrite the calm part.
The branch that lives too long starts telling a different story.
Documentation that matches the code is a feature.
The first version should be easy to delete.
A failing test is a question the code must answer.
Names that tell the truth reduce the need for meetings.
The edge case you skip will introduce itself in production.
Leave the code a little clearer than you found it.
A green build can still be describing the wrong behaviour.
The silent retry will hide the failure until it is too large.
A shared mutable value is waiting for two callers to meet.
The migration you postponed has started keeping score.
An unbounded queue is a polite way to run out of memory.
The feature flag you meant to remove has become a second product.
Credentials in a chat log do not stay in the chat.
A catch that ignores the error will not ignore the consequence.
The clock on one server has already drifted from the others.
Copying the config by hand will copy the mistake as well.
The cache you trust has not heard about the latest write.
A partial deploy leaves two versions explaining themselves at once.
The test that always passes has stopped being a test.
Disk space ends during the backup you were counting on.
A timeout that is too long looks healthy until the pile tips over.
A force push rewrites the story the reviewer already read.
The default password is still the default on the box you forgot.
Skipping the index will be fine until the table grows up.
The alert with no owner will ring for nobody.
Two services writing the same row will eventually disagree in public.
The script that worked once has no memory of why.
An expired certificate prefers a Friday.
The log line you removed was the only witness.
A wide open security group is not a temporary convenience.
The rollback you have not rehearsed is only a rumour.
A function named temporary will celebrate an anniversary.
The ticket you deferred will return with friends.
Someone will ask for the one-off report every week.
The prototype will be demonstrated to a customer.
A dependency bump will rearrange a screen you did not mean to touch.
The small refactor will reveal a second, older refactor.
You will find the answer in a commit message from last year.
A flaky test will pass the moment you start to describe it.
The config value nobody remembers will become load-bearing.
You will automate the task the third time you do it by hand.
A reviewer will ask the question you hoped the diff already answered.
The migration will need one more column than the plan allowed.
You will meet this bug again under a different stack trace.
The dashboard will be screenshotted into a slide.
A shortcut in the build will become the official path.
The estimate will be quoted back to you without the conditions.
You will rediscover a helper that already does the thing.
The incident write-up will be the best documentation this service gets.
A quiet service will become noisy the week you are away.
The sample data will escape into a real environment.
You will rename the variable and finally understand the function.
The backlog item marked minor will unblock three other teams.
A comment that says do not remove will be removed.
The next outage will rhyme with one you have already seen.
You will be grateful for the test you almost skipped.
The repository has started referring to itself in the third person.
A file named final-final has appeared in the root.
The build log contains a sentence that was not printed by the build.
Somewhere a cron job is still proud of an old year.
The staging database knows your name.
An empty directory is watching the deploy.
The linter has opinions about code that is not open.
A breakpoint you removed has been seen in the production logs.
The README and the code have stopped speaking.
One container is healthy in a way the others find concerning.
The ticket has no author and a very specific due date.
A stack trace ends in a function nobody admits to writing.
The monitor is green because it stopped asking.
Your editor scrolled to a line you have never visited.
The backup completed in a suspiciously cheerful amount of time.
A config key is set to yes, but yes is not the word you think.
The branch list is longer than the team.
Something in the temp directory has a lock file and a plan.
The graph flattened because the metric gave up.
A comment says it works if you do not look directly at it.
The service restarted itself and did not leave a note.
Two clocks in the cluster have chosen different afternoons.
The test fixture contains a date that has not happened yet.
An old reminder was checked off by a commit that only changed whitespace.
The on-call phone already knows you are reading this.
You are allowed to make the change smaller and still be brave.
Asking for the context is part of doing the work well.
The fact that you noticed the smell means you can improve it.
A careful rollback is a kind of success.
You do not have to understand everything to leave one path clearer.
Rest is a legitimate step in debugging.
The reviewer who asks questions is helping you ship.
You can delete the experiment. The learning stays.
Progress that is honest is faster than progress that is performed.
You have fixed harder things than this ticket suggests.
Writing the failing test first is a vote of confidence in yourself.
It is fine to say you need the afternoon to do this properly.
The messy draft is how the clean version begins.
You are not behind. You are in the middle, which is where work happens.
Pairing is not a confession. It is a shortcut to a better idea.
Your questions make the design safer for the next person.
Shipping a slice today is a gift to tomorrow.
You can be proud of the bug you prevented, even if nobody sees it.
The code does not need you to be brilliant. It needs you to be clear.
Take the walk. The stack trace will still be there, and kinder.
You are building something people will rely on. That is worth care.
A well-named function is a small act of hospitality.
You can ask for help before you are stuck. That is experience.
The careful commit you make today will help a noisy afternoon.
You belong in this codebase. Leave a sign that you were kind to it.
DNS has decided to become a philosophy.
The certificate expires on a day when everyone is in a workshop.
The container is fine. The network policy has not met it yet.
Helm rendered a value that nobody put in the values file on purpose.
The pipeline is red on a step whose owner is a distribution list.
Kubernetes moved the pod to a node with different opinions.
The health check passes if you do not ask it to do any work.
Terraform wants to replace the thing you only meant to rename.
The secret was rotated, and the old pod is the last to hear.
A volume mounted the directory you were using for notes.
The canary is happy and the stable track is still negotiating.
CI spent eight minutes installing a compiler for a five-line check.
The load balancer is sending traffic into yesterday's task definition.
Your manifest is valid YAML and slightly invalid intentions.
The rollback plan is a link to a document from the previous rollback.
Prometheus is graphing a metric that means three different things.
The ingress and the service have never been formally introduced.
A cron job in the cluster still believes in an old fileserver.
The image tag latest has been latest since the previous incident.
Disk pressure evicted the one pod that was doing something useful.
The deploy froze because a webhook returned an unexpected body.
Two regions are healthy and disagree about which release is current.
The readiness probe is ready. The application is still starting.
You exported the dashboard, and it exported your assumptions too.
The pipeline passed because a historical edit skipped the test stage.
The function is long, and only a few lines are the actual point.
A null checked three times is a design asking for a type.
The test name says what, and the assertion says something else.
You fixed the bug in the copy of the function, not the function.
The dependency update brought a new default and an old surprise.
This loop is searching a collection that already knows the answer.
The boolean argument has become a small undocumented mode switch.
The parser accepts the input and apologises in the next function.
A magic number in the middle of the method is a hidden requirement.
The mock returns the shape the test wants, not the one production sends.
You can extract a function here without inventing a framework.
The exception handler is broader than the mistake it meant to catch.
Two tests pass by sharing a global that production does not have.
The regex is correct and also a request for a real parser.
The comment says obvious. The next reader would like a noun.
This class has a constructor, a secret second one, and a hope.
The off-by-one is hiding in the range that looked friendly.
Formatting the code revealed that two branches do the same thing.
The helper you inlined last month wants to be a helper again.
A stringly typed status will collect new spellings.
The fixture builds a world so large the assertion cannot see the bug.
You do not need a new abstraction. You need the old one to be honest.
The log line will include a secret if the error takes the long path.
Renaming this variable makes the conditional boring, which is the goal.
The code is clever in a way the on-call rotation will not enjoy.
The meeting invite has an agenda, which is already a good sign.
Your next piece of feedback will be about a decision you can explain.
A promotion packet is a story with links, not a list of sufferings.
The interview question is really asking how you handle uncertainty.
Someone will praise the diff that made the system calmer.
You will be asked to estimate a thing that is still a metaphor.
The mentor you need is nearby and also busy. Ask anyway.
A title does not debug a race condition.
The presentation will go better if the demo can fail without you.
Your one-to-one is a good place to say what you want to learn next.
The work that looks invisible is often the work that kept Friday quiet.
You can decline a meeting that has no decision hiding in it.
The recruiter message is not a performance review.
A clear no saves more time than a vague yes.
A more senior title, if it comes, will still involve stack traces.
Write down the win before the week convinces you it was normal.
The best collaborators leave the ticket easier than they found it.
You are allowed to want work that is interesting and also finished.
A design doc is a kindness to the people who were not in the room.
The talk you fear is just a README with an audience.
Your manager cannot help with a problem they have not heard.
Switching teams will not switch off your taste.
The calendar is full. The priority is still yours to name.
A good code review is a professional act, not a personality.
You will be proud of the engineer you are on an ordinary Tuesday.
The deployment can wait. Your weekend cannot.
Friday afternoon is a poor time to meet a new migration.
If the rollback is a theory, Monday is the experiment.
Ship the documentation. Leave the surprise for a weekday.
The green button looks friendlier after lunch than it will at dusk.
A small fix can stay small until Monday.
The reviewer who already left is not a blocker. They are a sign.
Production has weekend plans that do not include your refactor.
Write down where you stopped. The next session starts in daylight.
The flaky test will not become stable out of respect for Friday.
Merge the typo. Schedule the architecture.
If you would not start it on Monday morning, do not start it now.
The deploy window and the train home are having a conversation.
A feature flag that defaults to off is a very Friday decision.
Leave a note in the ticket. Heroics do not page well.
The build is green enough to walk away from.
Nobody will thank you for a puzzle that arrives with the weekend.
Close the laptop on a known state.
The urgent request can survive a sentence that says Monday.
Your future on-call self is asking for a dull Friday.
A branch named after Friday is the start of a ghost story.
Tests that pass locally can keep passing without a deploy.
The rollback script you have not read is not yet a plan.
Choose the version of this change that fits before people log off.
Go home while the graphs are boring. Boring is the prize.
